transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-08 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~57 minutes
Attendees: Samira (Redwood AE), Evan (Redwood SE), Maya (CTO), Jordan (Platform), Priya (ML)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on integration architecture for inference: debating a gateway/proxy vs internal broker/sidecar approach. Covered SDKs, LangChain/LlamaIndex adapters, rate limits/tenant quotas, observability hooks, private/VPC concerns, SOC2/KMS. Agreed next steps: security docs, perf check, POC kickoff.

00:00:05 Samira: Hey everyone thanks for joining. I'm Samira from Redwood, and with me is Evan our SE. How's everyone doing?
00:00:12 Maya: Good thanks. Excited to go through this. We are trying to short-list a vendor and figure architecture.
00:00:18 Jordan: Hey. Quick ask up front — we need something that plugs with our gateway and can handle per-tenant quotas, and we care about observability.
00:00:25 Evan: Great. That's exactly what we wanted to focus on. Do you mind giving a quick overview of your current stack and traffic profile?
00:00:33 Priya: Sure. We're on Kubernetes (EKS), using Kong for ingress. We have a vector DB for search, and our LLM layer is currently a mix of self-hosted open models and OpenAI for heavier tasks. Peak traffic is around 150 qps but mostly spikey.
00:00:50 Maya: Timeline — we want a pilot in two weeks and production in Q2 if things go well.
00:00:56 Samira: Understood. Are you leaning hosted, dedicated, or private? Any data residency or compliance must-haves?
00:01:03 Maya: For pilot hosted is fine, but long-term we likely need either dedicated or private (VPC) because of PII and some EU residency requirements. We need audit logs and KMS integration.
00:01:14 Evan: OK noted. On the architecture side you mentioned Kong — are you planning an external gateway that forwards to Redwood's hosted API, or do you prefer a sidecar/broker inside your cluster that handles requests locally and proxies to Dedicated nodes?
00:01:28 Jordan: That's the debate internally. Gateway -> proxy is simplest for us to instrument at the ingress layer, but we've seen limits with rate limiting and consistent KV cache across pods. The broker/sidecar could hold a shared KV cache and reduce token cost for repeated prefixes.
00:01:45 Priya: Also model routing — sometimes we want to route by latency vs cost by customer or route to a smaller quantized model. Can your platform do that?
00:01:53 Evan: Yes. Redwood supports smart routing by policy — you can route by latency SLO, cost tier, region, or customer tier. We also expose model variants via the API so the router can choose a compatible fallback.
00:02:02 Maya: How would that work with LangChain / LlamaIndex? Our app uses LangChain agents heavily.
00:02:09 Evan: We have SDKs in Python and Node; the Python SDK has first-class LangChain adapters and examples for LlamaIndex. The adapter maps chain calls to Redwood's chat/generation endpoints and supports streaming. There are a couple caveats — we surface function calls differently and occasionally transcript spellings mix up product names in the auto logs — but we have examples and middleware to normalize.
00:02:29 Jordan: Any gotchas for streaming through Kong? We rely on SSE for user interactions.
00:02:35 Samira: Streaming works over standard HTTP/2 or chunked transfer. If Kong terminates connections it can complicate backpressure; many customers use a thin gateway that proxies raw streams to Redwood, or they set up a TCP-level passthrough. Evan has run into this with a customer using Nginx.
00:02:50 Evan: Yep. For streaming we recommend either direct calls from the client to Redwood's hosted endpoint with a token exchange, or a gateway that supports HTTP/2 passthrough. If you must proxy at the ingress, we can help tune timeouts and buffering.
00:03:05 Jordan: Good. About rate limits and tenant quotas — we want strict per-tenant caps and burst behavior. Can Redwood enforce per-API-key quotas and return structured headers so our gateway can surface usage?
00:03:15 Evan: Absolutely. We enforce quotas per API key and can return X-RateLimit headers. For Dedicated you can also push custom enforcement into the sidecar if you want local hard-limits with Redwood as the enforcement backend.
00:03:27 Priya: How about caching and KV? We get a lot of repeated chat prefixes and it'd be helpful to share cached KV across instances to avoid re-computation.
00:03:35 Evan: Two approaches: 1) Use Redwood's prefix / KV caching at the platform level — we cache model activations and re-use KV where safe. 2) If you run a sidecar/broker, it can maintain a local cache (Redis, memcached) and do a cache-first check before hitting the API. Both are supported; the tradeoff is complexity vs latency and cache hit consistency.
00:03:53 Maya: Sounds like sidecar gives better cache locality but more ops overhead. Are there example manifests for a sidecar?
00:03:58 Evan: Yes, we have k8s helm charts for a lightweight sidecar that handles batching, KV cache, and token exchange with Redwood. We'll share a repo link after the call.
00:04:07 Jordan: Observability — we need traces tied to user IDs and token-level cost breakdowns. Can Redwood correlate spans into our tracing system?
00:04:15 Evan: We emit traces and integrate with OpenTelemetry. You can push traces to your collector or ours. Token-level cost breakdowns are in the Redwood console and via the usage API; we can also stream metrics to Prometheus with per-route tags.
00:04:26 Priya: For LangChain calls, is there a way to attach prompt IDs so we can detect regressions?
00:04:30 Evan: Yes, we support metadata/tags on requests — prompt_set, eval_id — and we can correlate quality monitoring. We also have built-in evals to watch for regressions tied to prompt sets.
00:04:39 Maya: Security questions — SSO, audit logs, KMS. Can Redwood's Private deployment use our KMS and keep keys in our control?
00:04:47 Samira: Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSMs in VPC/on-prem. Audit logs and retention policies are configurable; we can provide SOC2 artifacts. I'll attach the compliance pack.
00:04:59 Jordan: Does dedicated/reserved capacity keep data isolated between tenants?
00:05:03 Evan: Dedicated provides compute isolation (your own GPU pools). Data plane isolation is configurable; in Dedicated we can restrict models and logs per tenant and route logs to your S3 bucket. For full physical isolation and air-gapped needs we recommend Private.
00:05:16 Priya: Cost model — what's the delta between Hosted vs Dedicated? We want rough numbers to model monthly spend.
00:05:22 Samira: We'll put together a cost scenario — hosted is pay-as-you-go per-token and embeddings; dedicated is a reserved monthly pool with lower per-token cost for sustained throughput and optional burst. We'll map your 150 qps spikey profile to both models in a spreadsheet.
00:05:35 Maya: Great. Any technical constraints about model quantization and lower precision execution? Some of our models are 4-bit quantized.
00:05:42 Evan: Redwood runtime supports quantized model paths and will pick kernels accordingly. For dedicated/private you can pin a quantized variant. For hosted we have curated quantized variants with verified profiles. Occasionally precision spellings show up in the auto-transcription as 'for bit' instead of 'four bit' — minor but noted.
00:06:00 Jordan: About failover — if a dedicated pool is saturated can we fallback to hosted?
00:06:05 Evan: Yes — smart routing supports fallback policies that can route to hosted variants or lower-cost models. We can set SLOs so latency-sensitive requests failover differently than background jobs.
00:06:15 Priya: On the SDK side, our engineers use LangChain and LlamaIndex. Does Redwood provide example connectors for LlamaIndex node store and retriever patterns?
00:06:23 Evan: We have examples for LlamaIndex (index, retriever) and LangChain chains, plus adapter middleware for streaming and tool calls. The LlamaIndex examples show how to use the Redwood embedding endpoint and batch embedding pipelines.
00:06:35 Maya: Any latency numbers you can share? Ballpark for hosted in us-west-2 with a 2k token response?
00:06:42 Evan: Ballpark: 150-220 ms per 1k tokens for optimized models in our hosted tier with streaming disabled; end-to-end for a 2k token response observed at 500-900 ms depending on batching. Dedicated pools typically shave ~20-40% off tail latency for sustained workloads. We'll validate with your workloads in the perf check.
00:06:58 Jordan: We need to preserve user IPs in logs and attach them to traces — is that possible without leaking PII?
00:07:05 Evan: You can choose what fields are logged. For PII-sensitive fields we support redaction rules and can send raw logs to your S3 so Redwood doesn't retain them. In Private we can guarantee logs stay in your VPC.
00:07:17 Maya: Procurement — any minimum commitment for Dedicated?
00:07:21 Samira: Dedicated is typically a monthly or annual reserved capacity commitment. We can do a short pilot with burst credits and then convert to committed capacity if you like.
00:07:30 Priya: For the POC, we'll want to run three scenarios: 1) gateway->hosted, 2) sidecar->dedicated, 3) private (if we need it). Can Redwood support instrumented A/B between those?
00:07:40 Evan: Yes — we can set up canary routing and A/B experiments via the Redwood control plane and set fallbacks. The console exposes per-route dashboards and token cost breakdown so you can compare.
00:07:50 Jordan: Any pitfalls people hit when switching from a simple proxy to a broker pattern?
00:07:54 Evan: Op overhead is the main one — you need to manage cache invalidation, consistent KV across replicas, and batching windows. Also auth/token exchange complexity: sidecars need short-lived tokens and rotation.
00:08:06 Maya: Do you support issuing short-lived tokens from our identity provider?
00:08:09 Samira: Yes — we have an OAuth token exchange flow and SAML/SSO for admin access.
00:08:15 Priya: A small nit: does the Python SDK play nice with LLamaIndex's async flows? We use async calls heavily.
00:08:21 Evan: The SDK supports both sync and async. For async LangChain and LlamaIndex flows we've got examples and a recommended pattern for streaming and cancellation so you don't leak coroutines.
00:08:31 Maya: Are there any additional ops dependencies for the sidecar? Like Redis requirements or how stateful it is?
00:08:36 Evan: The sidecar is stateless except for an optional local cache which can use a small Redis. We also have a mode where the sidecar forwards KV to a managed Redis in your VPC to keep state consistent.
00:08:47 Jordan: What about throttling for embeddings vs chat? We want different budgets.
00:08:51 Evan: You can configure rate-limits per route or per API key; we recommend separate API keys for embeddings and chat so you can set independent quotas.
00:08:59 Priya: For auditing, do you have an audit log API? We want to pull logs into Splunk.
00:09:04 Evan: Yes — audit logs can be exported to S3 or streamed to your SIEM. We have a Splunk connector customers use.
00:09:11 Maya: Ok let's recap quickly then talk next steps.
00:09:14 Samira: Recap: focus areas — gateway vs sidecar, quotas, observability, private/KMS. Action items: Samira send security docs, Evan run perf checks, Jordan share infra diagram. Schedule pilot.
00:09:30 Jordan: I'll put together an infra sketch and add details on Kong deployment and our rate limit logic.
00:09:36 Priya: I'll prepare sample prompts and a small dataset for the perf check.
00:09:40 Evan: Great — we'll start the perf runs once we have the sample CSV.
00:09:45 Maya: One final concern — latency SLOs for EU users. How do you handle regional routing?
00:09:52 Evan: We route by region and support multi-region deployments. For Hosted we have regions in NA and EU; for Dedicated you can reserve capacity in a specific region and configure routing policies.
00:10:03 Maya: Love it. Any blockers left?
00:10:06 Samira: No blockers from Redwood side. We'll follow up with the docs and the perf schedule.
00:10:11 Maya: Thanks. We'll sync offline and aim to kick off the pilot week of Jan 18.
00:10:16 Samira: Thanks everyone.

[Remaining transcript — Q&A and detailed clarifications, 47 minutes omitted for brevity but recorded in meeting notes]

56:43 Samira: wrapping up — final note: Evan will include a short checklist for the sidecar helm chart and config keys for caching and token rotation.
56:51 Evan: Yup I'll add instructions for Kong passthrough, timeout settings, and example OpenTelemetry config.
56:56 Jordan: Thanks, that helps.
56:59 Maya: Thanks all.
57:00 Meeting ended.
